newsitem.title: USA: US CREDIT OUTLOOK - Payrolls take center stage Fri.
newsitem.headline: US CREDIT OUTLOOK - Payrolls take center stage Fri.

text.p: U.S. bond market players awaited the crucial May nonfarm payrolls report on Friday for direction on prices.

Economists polled by Reuters expected, on average, that nonfarm payrolls would rise by 219,000 given the Bureau of Labor Statistics' seasonal revisions announced last Friday. That was a small decline from the original consensus for a rise of 221,000.
Average hourly earnings were seen rising by 0.4 percent, and the average workweek was seen increasing to 34.7 hours.

Flanagan said average hourly earnings could rise by 0.4 percent, but regardless of the percentage wages were sure to rise. But that would not necessarily push the Federal Reserve to tighten monetary policy, he said.
Instead, the Fed would be looking to an assortment of economic indicators such as retail sales and strength in the manufacturing and housing sectors, he said.
"It's 50/50 right now on whether they tighten in July," Flanagan said. "But it should be noted that they have never tightened in July in the 1990s," he said.

Kevin Flanagan, vice president and money market economist at Dean Witter Reynolds Inc, noted that the market didn't seem to be anticipating Friday's employment report with much trepidation. However, he noted that strikes and weather affected the April numbers and those factors would play much less of a role in May.

"We're scaling back our original estimate of a 275,000 gain to 225,000 to 250,000 due to the recalibration of the seasonal adjustments," Flanagan said. "But the labor market remains very strong right now."

"Market price numbers are telling us (nonfarm payroll will increase) 220,000, but the numbers are all over the lot," said Michael McClure, head of government securities trading at Zions First National Bank in Salt Lake City, Utah.
Numbers substantially below that level obviously would spike bond prices higher, he said, and Zions was only looking for a gain of 175,000.

McClure saw the Fed remaining on the sidelines at its July policy-making meeting as growth should slow to 2.5 percent to 5.0 percent in the second quarter, down from the first quarter's unsustainable pace of 5.8 percent.
The House on Thursday gave final approval to a budget deficit agreement intended to bring the federal shortfall to zero by by the year 2002 and cut taxes by $85 billion.
However, the Senate still had to vote on the measure -- where approval was expected -- and President Clinton had to sign off on the legislation.

The agreement had little effect on Treasury prices late Thursday afternoon, however, in front of the nonfarm payrolls report. Analysts said a budget agreement had already been factored into Treasury prices.
